policy.purpose: Evidence ledger for canonical Pattern Dictionary Wave 2 before any runtime publication.
policy.primary_palette_rule: A fixed primary palette is an editorial recognition reference unless a source establishes color as identity-relevant. It is never presented as the only valid colorway.
policy.relationship_rule: similar and often_confused_with are visual-discovery relationships, not claims of shared historical origin unless explicitly sourced.
policy.qualification_rule: Use qualified when the market term, textile/style convention, weave/effect category, or modern usage does not resolve to one uniquely fixed motif.

patterns.term_scope: named large-scale red-and-black check convention

verified_names.ja: バッファローチェック

ja: バッファローチェック柄

patterns.structure: A large, evenly spaced two-color check; the canonical recognition reference is the familiar red-and-black version.

color_guidance.reason: Red-and-black is the historically documented and dominant recognition convention, while the geometry remains the key structural cue.

patterns.term_scope: small even check family

ja: シェパードチェック柄

patterns.structure: Small, even checks formed by contrasting stripes, classically black and white.

color_guidance.reason: Black-and-white is explicitly documented as a classic construction, but the pattern family is not restricted to one palette.

supports: relationship to later district and gun-club checks

patterns.term_scope: large-scale thin-line check

verified_names.ja: ウィンドウペーンチェック

patterns.structure: Thin horizontal and vertical lines intersect at wide intervals to form large square or rectangular panes.

color_guidance.reason: The pane-like grid and large scale define the recognition target, not a fixed color.

supports: use as overcheck in Prince of Wales/tartan

patterns.term_scope: Madras textile/check style rather than one fixed grid specification
patterns.structure: A woven cotton check/plaid style associated with Madras/Chennai textiles, commonly recognized through relatively large multicolor crossing stripes.

color_guidance.reason: Multicolor plaid is a strong modern recognition cue, but sources do not support one exclusive palette.

patterns.qualification: Madras is also a cloth/textile term and historical textile tradition, not a single immutable check geometry. Detail copy must not present one reference repeat as the only authentic Madras pattern.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture

patterns.term_scope: thin-line multicolor check on a light ground

ja: タッターソールチェック
タッタソールチェック

patterns.structure: Thin colored crossbars form repeated squares on a solid, usually light background; multiple stripe colors are common.

color_guidance.reason: Light ground plus multiple thin colored lines is a stronger recognition cue than any one palette.

patterns.term_scope: multicolor district-check family derived from shepherd-check variation

ja: ガンクラブチェック柄

patterns.structure: A small repeating check using multiple tones/colors, commonly understood as a shepherd-check or related base varied with additional colors/check layers.

color_guidance.reason: Multiple contrasting tones are characteristic, but exact colors vary across gun-club checks.

patterns.term_scope: glen-check-derived check convention with modern naming overlap

verified_names.ja: プリンス・オブ・ウェールズ・チェック

ja: プリンスオブウェールズチェック

patterns.structure: A glen-check-like tight compound check commonly distinguished by a larger contrasting windowpane overcheck.

color_guidance.reason: Neutral glen-like base plus a contrasting overcheck is a useful recognition reference, not a universal color rule.

patterns.qualification: Modern sources often use Prince of Wales Check and Glen Check interchangeably, while historical and tailoring references distinguish Prince of Wales through an added overcheck or specific lineage. Detail copy must state both the practical distinction and the naming overlap.

supports: modern naming overlap with glen check
glen-check base plus windowpane overcheck as practical distinction

patterns.term_scope: very narrow parallel stripe pattern in cloth
patterns.structure: Very narrow, usually pale parallel stripes on a darker cloth, especially associated with tailoring.

color_guidance.reason: Pale narrow lines on a dark ground are well documented, but exact colors are variable.

patterns.term_scope: wider softer parallel stripe convention used in suiting

ja: チョークストライプ柄

patterns.structure: Parallel pale stripes on a dark ground, wider and generally softer/more muted in appearance than pinstripes.

color_guidance.reason: White/pale lines on dark cloth are conventional; width/softness relative to pinstripe is the stronger distinction.

patterns.term_scope: balanced alternating colored-and-white stripe convention

ja: ベンガルストライプ柄

patterns.structure: Evenly spaced stripes of alternating color and white, typically broader than fine pin/pencil stripes.

color_guidance.reason: Alternating white and color is structural; blue is only a familiar recognition reference.

patterns.term_scope: broad Japanese lattice/check family
patterns.structure: Vertical and horizontal stripes/lines intersect to form a lattice of rectangular or square cells; many named subtypes vary line weight, count, and spacing.

color_guidance.reason: Line intersection defines the family; color is not intrinsic.

patterns.qualification: Koushi/格子 is a broad Japanese pattern family with many variants, not one unique repeat. Detail copy must distinguish this line-based lattice family from Ichimatsu's alternating filled squares.

sources.publisher: Agency for Cultural Affairs / Cultural Heritage Online

supports: 格子 included among Japanese geometric continuous patterns

sources.publisher: National Diet Library Collaborative Reference Database

patterns.term_scope: very broad stripe convention named after awnings

verified_names.ja: オーニングストライプ

ja: オーニングストライプ柄

patterns.structure: Bold, broad, regularly repeated stripes recalling traditional shop or outdoor awnings.

color_guidance.reason: Large stripe scale is defining; exact color is variable.

patterns.term_scope: stripe style associated with English/British regimental ties rather than one fixed repeat

verified_names.ja: レジメンタルストライプ

patterns.structure: A repeated stripe arrangement recognizable through its relationship to striped British regimental neckwear; exact widths, colors, and direction vary.

color_guidance.reason: Specific color sequences may carry organizational meaning, so the reference palette must not be presented as universal.

patterns.qualification: Regimental Stripe is a style/family label tied to regimental neckwear conventions, not one universal color sequence, stripe width, or direction. The dictionary must avoid assigning one generic stripe as an authentic regiment-specific design.

patterns.term_scope: French maritime clothing/style convention derived from striped naval knitwear
patterns.structure: Horizontal contrasting stripes, classically blue/navy and white, strongly associated with the French maritime/Breton top tradition.

color_guidance.reason: Blue-and-white horizontal striping is central to the historic naval reference, while modern Breton-style garments vary spacing and colors.

patterns.qualification: The historic French naval garment had specific uniform dimensions, but modern 'Breton stripe' is a broader fashion convention. Detail copy must distinguish the historical marinière specification from contemporary Breton-style stripes.

patterns.term_scope: dotted Swiss textile/fabric category, not generic printed polka dots
patterns.structure: Fine, sheer, crisp fabric carrying small dots on its surface; the dots may be woven, embroidered, flocked, or otherwise applied depending on the textile.

color_guidance.reason: Texture and dotted surface treatment matter more than color; white-on-white is a neutral recognition reference.

patterns.qualification: Swiss Dot/Dotted Swiss fundamentally names a dotted fabric/textile treatment. The dictionary must not collapse it into ordinary flat printed polka dots, and the reference image should convey textile surface/relief.

patterns.term_scope: herringbone weave/arrangement and its broken-V visual family
patterns.structure: Adjacent rows of short slanting strokes reverse direction to form repeated broken V shapes or zigzag columns.

color_guidance.reason: Direction reversal and broken-V structure define recognition; color is variable.

patterns.qualification: Herringbone can denote a textile weave, a broader visual arrangement, embroidery, brickwork, and other constructions. In Pattern Dictionary it is represented as the visual family while clearly distinguishing the common woven form from a simple printed Chevron/Zigzag.

supports: herringbone as a weave variation on twill

patterns.term_scope: generic angular line/pattern family
patterns.structure: A line or repeated pattern that changes direction at sharp angles, visually resembling joined Z shapes.

color_guidance.reason: Angular path geometry, not color, defines the generic family.

patterns.term_scope: generic repeated diamond/rhombus geometric family
patterns.structure: Repeated diamond/rhombus shapes, typically four-sided forms with equal sides and acute/obtuse opposite angles rather than a required color or internal line system.

color_guidance.reason: The repeated rhombus geometry defines the family.

supports: historic textile use of a repeated/stepped diamond pattern

patterns.term_scope: diamond-block pattern convention associated with Harlequin costume
patterns.structure: A repeated field of contrasting diamond-shaped blocks, drawing its recognition identity from Harlequin's diamond-patterned costume tradition.

color_guidance.reason: Contrasting diamond blocks are characteristic; no single modern palette is universal.

patterns.term_scope: generic alternating dark/light square pattern
patterns.structure: Dark and light squares alternate in a regular grid like a board used for checkers/draughts.

color_guidance.reason: Alternation of contrasting square values is defining, while black/white is only the clearest reference.
